title: Constraining the timescale of activity in Mrk 1018
abstract: We present analysis of an extended emission line region projected 3.77 kpc from the nucleus of the canonical changing-look AGN Mrk~1018, found in MUSE integral-field observations from the Close AGN Reference Survey. Emission-line ratios show that the region exhibits AGN ionisation but has a very low velocity dispersion, $77 \pm 1$ kms$^{-1}$, ruling out an ionised outflow. The lower limit on the light travel time is $12{,}300 \pm 2{,}300$ yr, implying that the nucleus has therefore been active for at least this long. This is much longer than the duration of either observed changing-look transition, which occurred over several years. This implies that Mrk 1018's multi-year variations are occurring within a longer term active phase.
reference: Rebecca McElroy, Scott M. Croom, Thomas Dunn (2026), arXiv:2611.07533.

title: FALCON (FERMI-ALMA Calibrator ObservatioN): Cross-matching ALMA Calibrators with Fermi-LAT Blazars
abstract: Blazars are active galactic nuclei with relativistic jets closely aligned with our line of sight, producing Doppler-boosted emission from radio to gamma rays. Millimeter emission near the synchrotron self-absorption turnover probes compact regions at the jet base, yet large statistical studies in this regime remain limited. We construct the FALCON (FERMI--ALMA Calibrator ObservatioN) catalogue, a millimeter-selected blazar sample by cross-matching the ALMA Calibrator Source Catalogue with the Third Data Release of the Fourth LAT AGN Catalog (4LAC-DR3). After removing duplicates, we obtain 949 unique gamma-ray-associated sources, corresponding to approximately 25 % of the 4LAC-DR3 blazar population. For the subset with available redshift measurements, we compute millimeter and gamma-ray luminosities and find a strong, statistically significant correlation that remains robust after accounting for redshift effects. Fermi-detected blazars exhibit systematically flatter millimeter spectral indices than gamma-ray non-detected ALMA calibrators, while the redshift-controlled luminosity correlation becomes progressively weaker from high-synchrotron-peaked BL Lacs toward flat-spectrum radio quasars. These results indicate an intrinsic connection between millimeter and gamma-ray emission, consistent with a common origin in relativistic jets governed by Doppler boosting and time-averaged jet power.
reference: Kanako Narita, Yoshiyuki Inoue, Bunyo Hatsukade et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.07737.

title: Confirming HSC strong lens candidates with DESI Spectroscopy. II. Analysis of 80 galaxy-scale systems with lens redshifts above 0.8
abstract: The total mass distribution of galaxies provides a sensitive probe of the fundamental physical processes governing galaxy evolution, including gas inflow/star formation, AGN/SN feedback, galaxy merging, and the nature of dark matter. State-of-the-art cosmological simulations have therefore made extensive predictions for the evolution of the total-mass density slope. Interestingly, their predictions diverge significantly at high redshift, primarily due to differences in how these key physical mechanisms are implemented. However, measurements of the total-mass structure evolution have been largely confined to low and intermediate redshifts, leaving the regime where model predictions differ most significantly (z>0.8) largely unexplored. In the first paper of this series, we reported the discovery of 84 candidate strong-lens systems with lens redshifts above 0.8. In this work, we perform lens modeling of the 80 galaxy-scale systems to assess their lensing nature. Of these, 71 systems (approximately 90%) exhibit clear lensing features that are well reproduced by our lens models and are therefore classified as secure strong lenses. Another eight systems are classified as probable (5) or possible (3) strong lenses, based on the prominence of their lensing features and the quality of the lens modeling. One system lacking reliable lensing features in current imaging data is classified as a non-lens. Our analysis nearly triples the number of known galaxy-scale strong lenses at z_lens > 0.8, making statistical studies of the total mass structure of high-redshift galaxies possible for the first time. This expanded sample provides an unprecedented opportunity to test the predictions of cosmological simulations and discriminate between competing physical prescriptions.
reference: Shen Li, Yiping Shu, Lin Nie (2026), arXiv:2611.07524.

title: Black Hole Seeds and Little Red Dots: Connecting Formation and Growth with a JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Program
abstract: JWST has revealed an abundant population of faint active galactic nuclei and a new class of compact, high-redshift sources known as Little Red Dots (LRDs), whose physical nature remains debated, with accreting massive black holes among the leading explanations. The emerging demographics of early black holes, with their high inferred number densities and, in some systems, the apparent excess of black hole mass relative to stellar mass, challenge simple scenarios of black hole seeding and growth. Despite these observational breakthroughs, the origin of early massive black holes remains uncertain, because "black holes have no memory": current samples cannot separate the imprint of seeding from subsequent growth. This white paper identifies the multi-cycle JWST observations needed to revolutionize our understanding of early black hole growth by: (i) distinguishing seeding pathways, (ii) constraining early black hole growth mechanisms, (iii) resolving the physical nature of broad-line emitters and LRDs, and (iv) testing black hole-galaxy co-evolution. These tasks require uniformly selected samples extending to low black hole and host-galaxy masses, allowing self-consistent measurements of black hole mass functions, Eddington-ratio distributions, and host properties. Grating spectroscopy, deep MIRI imaging, and variability analysis through repeated observations of the same fields would provide complementary tests of black hole formation and growth, their connection to host-galaxy evolution, and the nature of newly discovered populations of LRDs. In this white paper, we argue that these joint tests require a coordinated JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program; such a program could provide the depth, uniformity, and time baseline needed to place substantially stronger, complementary constraints on early black hole formation, growth, and their connection to galaxy evolution.
reference: Fabio Pacucci, Raffaella Schneider, Harley Katz et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.07006.

title: AGN Archaeology: A Systematic Search for Fading AGN in MaNGA
abstract: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) vary on broad timescales, but are primarily thought to "flicker" on and off during episodes of high and low accretion. Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) which are actively accreting material often show optical spectra dominated by AGN emission in their nuclei and beyond. In this work we develop an empirical model to quantify the fractional AGN contribution to optical spectra using the Baldwin-Phillips-Terlevich (BPT) emission line diagnostic diagram. We leverage this model against integral field unit (IFU) data from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) survey to select 34 galaxies with weak nuclear AGN activity relative to their AGN signatures at large radii; this signifies past AGN activity which is fading with time (i.e., fading-AGN). The majority of our fading-AGN reside in edge-on systems undergoing minor mergers. We construct a simple model consisting of a disk galaxy with ionization cones and find that the orientation of such a system will impact its BPT classification in both single-fiber and IFU observations. The mean distance to the extended AGN emission in our sample corresponds to a light-travel time of $1.1\times10^4$ years. We use this to set a lower-limit on the typical lifetime of the AGN phase ($t_{\text{AGN}}>1.3\times10^5$ years) which is consistent with SMBHs growing via brief accretion bursts. These fading-AGN allow us to probe the elusive period of post-AGN galaxy evolution, and they give a $\sim10^4$ year baseline for understanding the accretion history in these systems.
reference: Quinn O. Casey, Ryan C. Hickox, Jonathan H. Cohn et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.07028.

title: Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU): Selection of active galactic nuclei and star-formation emission with machine-learning techniques
abstract: Sources detected by recent large-area radio surveys require robust classification and characterisation. The Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) is a prime example of machine-learning (ML) techniques efficiently enriching existing catalogues with classifications and derived physical properties that would be impractical to obtain from spectroscopy or colour selection alone. We aim to build a labelled sample of sources in the EMU pilot survey (EMU-PS, at 944 MHz, with rms ~ 30 uJy/beam over 270 deg2 in the southern sky) classified as being dominated by active galactic nuclei (AGNs) or non-AGN processes including star-formation. We will then use this sample to examine radio properties and redshift-dependent trends. We applied a pre-trained multi-stage ML pipeline to optical-to-infrared photometry of EMU-PS sources to derive classifications and photometric redshifts, which we used to compute additional radio properties, including luminosities. We increase the known number of AGNs and non-AGNs in the EMU-PS by more than a factor of 15 (recall 96 %) up to z ~ 5, and by nearly a factor of 100 (recall 94 %) for z > 1, respectively. In extrapolating these numbers for the full EMU survey, we expect to recover more than 3.4 million AGN candidates. A non-negligible low-redshift subsample of selected non-AGNs shows radio luminosities in excess of those expected from star formation alone, revealing detachment between photometric and radio classification. Radio-derived properties show expected trends for luminosities and a lack of evolution for in-band (800-1088 MHz) spectral indices. The ML-based pipeline provides a scalable way to produce large catalogues for the ongoing EMU survey and future Square Kilometre Array observations and reveals that multi-wavelength analysis can uncover radio populations and trends often missed by colour cuts or spectroscopy alone.
reference: R. Carvajal, I. Matute, J. Afonso et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.06190.

title: The HST-Hyperion Survey: X-ray AGN Enhancement in the Hyperion Proto-supercluster
abstract: Dense environments can influence both galaxy evolution and supermassive black hole growth, but whether they enhance or suppress (or both) active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity at high redshift ($z\gtrsim2$) remains uncertain. As one of the most massive structures identified in the early universe, the Hyperion proto-supercluster at $z\approx2.5$ provides a unique opportunity to investigate this connection during an epoch near the peak of both cosmic star formation rate and AGN activity density. To examine the impact of galaxy environment on AGN activity, we measure the fraction of X-ray-selected AGN in Hyperion as a whole, its highly overdense peaks, and its outskirts, comparing these measurements to a coeval field sample. We identify X-ray AGN using the deep Chandra COSMOS-Legacy Survey and combine optical/near-infrared (NIR) photometry and photometric redshift information from COSMOS2020 with extensive ground-based spectroscopy and HST-grism observations. Redshift information is incorporated statistically using a Monte Carlo framework. We find a higher X-ray AGN fraction in Hyperion ($7.4^{+3.2}_{-1.8}\%$) than in the coeval field ($3.2^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\%$), corresponding to a $\sim2.3σ$ difference. Strikingly, this enhancement is concentrated in the overdense peaks, where the X-ray AGN fraction reaches $12.3^{+5.5}_{-3.4}\%$ ($15.0^{+6.9}_{-4.4}\%$ in the most massive peaks versus $6.2^{+11.9}_{-2.1}\%$ in the less massive peaks), while the lower-density Hyperion outskirts ($2.1^{+3.6}_{-1.1}\%$) show no evidence of enhancement relative to the field. These results add to the limited but growing evidence for enhanced AGN activity in high-redshift protostructures, suggesting that the dense environments at these epochs may preferentially trigger AGN during the early stages of cluster assembly.
reference: Ashlen Coburn, Finn Giddings, Derek Sikorski et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.07047.

title: ReveaLLAGN 3: Revealing the Infrared Spectral Energy Distributions of Low Luminosity AGN
abstract: The spectral energy distributions of active galactic nuclei (AGN) provide valuable information on the emission mechanisms taking place in their inner regions. Here we use the James Webb Space Telescope to study the near and mid-infrared spectral energy distributions of seven nearby low-luminosity active galaxy nuclei from 1.7 to 24 $μm$. We cleanly separate the AGN spectrum by performing spatial fits of the two-dimensional images across all wavelengths. We then compare these clean unresolved spectra to aperture-based spectra and show that they effectively remove galaxy contamination. Comparing our infrared measurements to X-ray emission, we find that low-luminosity AGN have enhanced near-infrared emission relative to more luminous AGN, a trend that correlates with radio-loudness, while their mid-infrared-to-X-ray ratios are comparable. A majority of our targets show strong compact silicate emission suggesting the presence of warm dust on parsec scales in these systems. We also quantify the near- and mid-infrared power-law slopes and colors of low-luminosity AGN. In the near-infrared we find AGN of all luminosities have similar spectral slopes and colors, however in the mid-infrared, we find low-luminosity AGN typically have steeper slopes and redder colors than more luminous AGN. Both the strong silicate emission and steep mid-infrared slopes disagree with existing models for low-luminosity AGN spectral energy distributions.
reference: David Ohlson, Anil C. Seth, Kameron Goold et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.06916.

title: AGN Host Galaxies in COSMOS-Web: Linking Structural Evolution and Star Formation Quenching up to $z=5$
abstract: The role of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in the suppression of star formation and structural evolution of galaxies during their transition from star-forming to quiescent systems remains unclear. We analyze 3,955 AGNs selected through five multiwavelength diagnostics at $0<z<5$. Using high-resolution JWST imaging from the COSMOS-Web survey and archival multi-wavelength photometry, we investigate the rest-frame optical size-mass distribution of AGN host galaxies and compare it with those of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and quiescent galaxies (QGs). We find that the positions of AGN hosts in the size-mass plane depend on both redshift and stellar mass. At $z\gtrsim2$, massive AGN hosts ($M_\star/M_\odot>10^{10.5}$) generally exhibit sizes comparable to those of SFGs despite suppressed star formation. Toward lower redshifts, they increasingly approach the QG size-mass relation, accompanied by declining specific star formation rates (sSFRs) and increasing Sérsic indices. In contrast, lower-mass AGN hosts remain close to the SFG relation across the redshift range. Overall, AGN hosts exhibit relatively mild size evolution, following $R_e\propto(1+z)^{-0.6}$ over $0<z<4$, shallower than that of typical SFGs and QGs. We further examine the relationship between star formation activity and structural compactness in the $Δ\log\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{MS}}$-$ΔΣ_e$ plane. At $z<2.2$, AGN hosts predominantly occupy the compact star-forming and quiescent regions, broadly consistent with the compaction-quenching scenario. At $z>2.2$, however, some AGN hosts exhibit suppressed star formation while retaining relatively extended structures. These findings suggest that some AGN hosts may follow alternative evolutionary pathways in which star formation suppression precedes substantial structural compaction.
reference: Xiao Han, Lilan Yang, T. Kelly et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.06443.

title: Aperture-dependent [O III] profile variability: Clues to the nature of double-peaked narrow emission lines
abstract: We propose a simple and practical aperture-dependent method for investigating the physical origin of double-peaked narrow emission lines (DPNELs). Spectroscopic observations obtained from different apertures probe different spatial regions and therefore different gas kinematics within the narrow line region (NLR). Consequently, changes in the profiles of DPNELs observed with different apertures can provide important constraints on their physical origins. We applied this method to SDSS J0941 by comparing spectra obtained from the SDSS, DESI, and LAMOST surveys. Significant differences are found in the double-peaked profiles of the different spectra, demonstrating that aperture effects can strongly influence the integrated DPNEL profiles. The AGN model, where the two nuclei lie in a plane perpendicular to the line of sight, can qualitatively explain the asymmetric sampling of the two NLRs, but it cannot explain the different peak separations of different spectra. The observed asymmetric evolution of the two components disfavors a simple AGN-driven outflow and a rotating disk-like NLR scenario. Of the models considered, only a more complex non-axisymmetric rotating NLR provides a self-consistent explanation for the observed aperture-dependent variations. In this scenario, the blueshifted emitting region is more compact and remains largely enclosed by the smaller aperture, resulting in an increased line width with little change in flux. In contrast, the redshifted emitting region is more spatially extended and is therefore more strongly affected by the reduced aperture, leading to pronounced decreases in both flux and line width. Our results illustrate the diagnostic potential of combining multi-aperture spectroscopic surveys to study DPNEL origins, while highlighting the difficulty of distinguishing between physical scenarios.
reference: Qi Zheng, Xingqian Chen, Zhegeng Chen et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.06150.

title: GetGaia 2.0: automatic membership and systemic motions of stellar systems with Gaia
abstract: We present GetGaia 2.0, a public Python package that retrieves the Gaia data around a stellar system and selects its member stars automatically. The membership is a probabilistic model fitted by expectation maximization that combines the astrometry of every source, with its full covariance, the color-magnitude diagram, the sky distribution and, when available, the line-of-sight velocities, from Gaia or from an external catalog. The local systematic errors of the Gaia reference frame are measured on the quasars of each field. The code returns the systemic proper motion (PM) and parallax with their full covariance, a detection significance, a contamination estimate and the structural parameters of the system. We validate it on synthetic catalogs, where it recovers the members with 90-100 percent purity, and run it on Gaia DR3 for the known dwarf galaxies of the Local Group within 850 kpc and for 95 Galactic globular clusters, in tiers that add one piece of literature information at a time. It measures the systemic PMs of 55 dwarf galaxies and 93 globular clusters at a significance of at least $3σ$; 29 of the dwarfs and 86 of the clusters are recovered from their position alone. The dwarfs include every Milky Way satellite within 300 kpc brighter than $M_V=-5.4$, ultra-faint systems down to $M_V=-0.8$, and nine galaxies at 370-820 kpc. The PMs agree with the published values within 0.1 mas/yr for 47 of the dwarfs and for all the clusters (median differences of 0.032 and 0.009 mas/yr), with uncertainties equal to those of dedicated studies, and none deviates by more than $3σ$. The Gaia line-of-sight velocities alone give the systemic velocity of 71 clusters, within 1 km/s of spectroscopy. GetGaia 2.0 delivers, without manual intervention, the systemic motions and the members of the stellar systems within the reach of Gaia, and is ready for the forthcoming Gaia data releases.
reference: Andrés del Pino (2026), arXiv:2611.07227.

title: A multi-epoch VLBI study of compact symmetric objects as contaminants in the search for milli-lenses
abstract: The Lambda Cold Dark Matter model predicts a high abundance of low-mass dark matter halos, which can be probed through milliarcsecond-scale gravitational lensing (milli-lensing) of background radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGNs). The Search for MIlli-LEnses (SMILE) project aims to find these rare systems with Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). However, compact symmetric objects (CSOs) can closely resemble milli-lenses in VLBI images and are the main contaminant in such searches. We aim to determine the nature of the nine remaining milli-lens candidates of the SMILE pilot study and to characterize their physical properties. We analyzed all available multi-epoch, multi-frequency archival VLBI data, new HSA and EVN observations, and single-dish and connected-element interferometer measurements. We tested the lensing hypothesis through the morphology and spectra of the sources, and characterized their kinematics, spatially resolved spectral indices, magnetic fields, and integrated spectra, using synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) and free-free absorption (FFA) models. We identify eight of the nine candidates as CSOs, four of them for the first time. Spectral index asymmetries between components and previously undetected emission connecting them rule out the lensing hypothesis. Only J0923-3435 remains ambiguous. For the CSOs with known redshifts, the lobes have equipartition magnetic fields of $\sim$20-320 mG and projected separations of $\sim$60-240 pc, and show no measurable expansion, implying kinematic ages of at least $\sim$50-950 yr. The integrated spectra of J0210-2213 and J2347-1856 favor an inhomogeneous external free-free absorber over homogeneous and inhomogeneous SSA models. Since CSOs will be the main contaminant in the full SMILE survey, applying this framework will provide the same constraints for a much larger sample of compact radio-loud AGNs.
reference: Diego Álvarez-Ortega, Felix M. Pötzl, Carolina Casadio (2026), arXiv:2611.07029.

title: The obscured nucleus of NGC3256 S. I. Anisotropic AGN near-IR radiation field traced by CO v=1-0 with JWST/NIRSpec
abstract: The southern nucleus of NGC3256, a nearby luminous infrared (IR) interacting system (d=40 Mpc; L(IR)=10^11.6 Lsun), hosts a deeply obscured low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) associated with a massive and fast bipolar collimated molecular outflow. JWST/NIRSpec observations revealed bright spatially resolved ro-vibrational CO v=1-0 4.67um emission at the base of this molecular outflow extending out to ~300pc, which is excited by the ~4.7um IR radiation from the southern dusty core. Using Monte Carlo radiative transfer (MCRT) models, we analyzed the CO v=1-0 band emission to determine the intensity of the ~4.7um IR radiation field across the outflow base. We find that the core spectral luminosity density at ~4.7um, as seen by the material in the outflow base, is ~2-4 times higher than that inferred along our line of sight, indicating an anisotropic near-IR radiation field. Moreover, the slower than d^-2 decrease of the near-IR flux density across the outflow base suggests a collimated radiation field, for which we estimate a small half-opening angle (15-20deg) and a diameter of the collimating structure of 15 +- 5 pc. This is slightly smaller than the diameter of the obscuring envelope (25 +- 5 pc). Combined with the expansion of this obscuring envelope, traced by the blueshifted CO v=1-0 absorption toward the nucleus, this suggests that the AGN is beginning to clear its environment. We estimate N_H~10^22-23 cm^-2 for NGC 3256 S, which is similar to that of Type 2 AGN. However, in contrast to Type 2 AGN, a high covering factor of the obscuring material, possibly sustained by inflows linked to the galaxy merger, and similar to that expected in deeply obscured compact obscured nuclei (CONs), is needed to explain the absence of extended high-ionization emission. Therefore, NGC 3256 S shares properties with CONs and Type 2 AGN.
reference: Miguel Pereira-Santaella, Eduardo González-Alfonso, Ismael García-Bernete et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.07020.

title: On the importance of medium-resolution continuum spectroscopy for JWST's extragalactic legacy
abstract: We argue for a significant investment of JWST time into an extremely deep medium-resolution NIRSpec MSA survey targeting a large, representative sample of high-redshift $(z>1.5)$ galaxies, specifically intended to obtain high-SNR continuum detections. This is only possible with JWST, and no planned future instrumentation has similar capabilities, meaning that obtaining such observations with JWST must be urgently prioritised. The vast majority of existing archival NIRSpec observations are not deep enough for continuum science, being focused on the detection of emission lines. Deeper continuum data opens up the ability to constrain a much wider range of key galaxy physical parameters, including stellar population ages and metallicities, stellar kinematics and neutral gas physical properties, inflows and outflows. Such measurements will provide crucial insight into quenching physics, galaxy dynamical masses, merger histories, pristine early star-formation, reionization and the physics of Little Red Dots, as well as enabling all of the emission-line science that can be achieved with shallower observations. To facilitate future survey planning, we present an empirically derived relationship between rest-optical continuum SNR in JWST NIRSpec medium-resolution data, rest-optical apparent magnitude and exposure time, which we show to be independent of redshift (and hence the grating used). We then provide a 1000-hour sketch survey plan based on achieving the continuum SNR $=20$/pixel necessary to constrain key physical properties and scaling relations for a large galaxy sample at $z>1.5$. We finally discuss NIRSpec sky subtraction strategies, which are of critical importance for continuum SNR.
reference: Adam C. Carnall, Ho-Hin Leung, Struan D. Stevenson et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.07070.

title: Constraining the white-dwarf mass in the intermediate polar IGR J17014-4306 using X-ray and optical spectroscopy
abstract: Intermediate polars (IPs), a subclass of magnetic cataclysmic variables, often show discrepancies between white-dwarf (WD) mass measurements from X-ray spectral modeling and optical dynamical studies. We investigate the IP IGR J17014-4306. We performed a joint spectral analysis of NuSTAR observations combined with archival XMM-Newton and Swift data, modeling the broad-band X-ray spectrum with a multi-temperature cooling-flow model. Additionally, we obtained time-resolved optical spectroscopy with the SOAR telescope to measure the radial velocity of the donor star and constrain the system's orbital parameters. The X-ray spectral analysis reveals a very high post-shock plasma temperature of $kT_{\max}=50_{-8}^{+11}\,\mathrm{keV}$, corresponding to a WD mass of $M_{\mathrm{WD}}=0.94_{-0.07}^{+0.09}\,M_\odot$. We also fitted the NuSTAR spectrum above 10 keV with the ipolar30KK model, obtaining $M_{\mathrm{WD}}=0.88_{-0.12}^{+0.14}\,M_\odot$. Our optical spectroscopy yields a radial-velocity semi-amplitude for the companion star of $K_2=165\pm4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and an optical mass function of $f(M)=0.249\pm0.018\,M_\odot$. Combined with the eclipse geometry and the WD mass estimate from the X-ray models, these results favor a high mass ratio, $0.76\lesssim q\lesssim0.95$, and a donor-star mass of approximately $0.67\lesssim M_2/M_\odot\lesssim0.89$. In the limiting case of $q=1$, the WD mass has an upper limit of $1.14\,M_\odot$. Together with the X-ray measurements, this indicates a relatively massive WD. The lack of an independent measurement of the WD dynamical mass leaves it unclear whether the dynamical mass is consistent with the X-ray measurements or whether the X-ray mass is underestimated, as has been found for other IPs. Thus, our constraints make IGR J17014-4306 an important system for improving our understanding of IPs.
reference: D. C. Souza, M. P. Diaz, A. S. Oliveira et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.06785.

title: Dust Survival in Lensed Quiescent Galaxies at $z>1$ Depends on How They Quench
abstract: The interstellar medium of massive quiescent galaxies holds key clues to how they quench, yet remain poorly understood. Although dust is expected to be depleted rapidly ($\lesssim$100 Myr) after quenching, some quiescent galaxies host substantial dust reservoirs, raising the question of whether dust survives quenching or is replenished afterward. We present ALMA Band 6 continuum observations ($λ_{\mathrm{rest}}$$>$250$μ$m) of eight strongly-lensed, spectroscopically-selected quiescent galaxies at z$\sim$1-2.5 from the COOL-LAMPS and REQUIEM surveys, plus five archival REQUIEM systems. The sample spans more than two orders of magnitude in dust-to-stellar-mass ratio ($f_{\mathrm{dust}}<10^{-5}$ to $>10^{-3}$), and two galaxies host extended, resolved dust. Comparing $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ with time since quenching, roughly half the sample, preferentially at higher redshift, is consistent with rapid quenching and harsh dust destruction, while lower-redshift, more slowly quenched systems are consistent with milder destruction, possibly reflecting an evolving dominant quenching mode. The two most dust-rich galaxies exceed even the mildest model destruction tracks, with J1201-3952 retaining the highest $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ $\sim$1.8 Gyr after quenching. If these systems are truly quiescent, their dust masses approach maximum stellar yields, pointing to ISM grain regrowth and/or TP-AGB dust production. However due to our single-band continuum data, $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ is uncertain ($\pm$0.3 dex systematic uncertainty from the unknown dust temperature) and we cannot rule out obscured star formation in these two galaxies. Our results suggest that dust survival depends on how galaxies quench: rapid, harsh quenching efficiently destroys dust, while slower, milder quenching can leave dust reservoirs that persist or are replenished long after star formation ceases.
reference: Sarah Bodansky, Katherine E. Whitaker, Gourav Khullar et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.07237.

title: Extreme Multiwavelength Variability in the Recurrent Intermediate-type Changing-look Seyfert Galaxy SDSS J234728.73+242745.7
abstract: We report the discovery of the Seyfert galaxy J234728.73+242745.7 as a recurrent intermediate-type CLAGN with extreme optical/UV variability. Optical spectra spanning nearly three decades reveal Type 1.0$\rightarrow$1.5$\rightarrow$1.2 transitions, accompanied by the disappearance and reappearance of broad He II $\lambda4686$ and a broad-line Balmer decrement evolving from 4.5 to 7.2 and then 2.4. Monitoring reveals coordinated variability from X-rays to the MIR. SED decomposition yields a host-corrected g-band high-to-low-state flux ratio of $5.4\pm0.4$, exceeding the Swift/XRT ratio of $2.7\pm0.8$ across the changing-look transition. This discrepancy may arise from reduced dust extinction, as correcting for the low-state continuum reddening ($A_V^{\rm cont}=0.66\pm0.23$ mag) brings the optical/UV ratios close to the X-ray value, although the correction is model-dependent and intrinsically weaker X-ray variability may also contribute. However, X-ray spectra show no compelling evidence for intrinsic gas absorption or its variability ($N_{\rm H}^{\rm intr}\lesssim5\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$). In contrast, EP/WXT monitoring during the recent high state reveals order-of-magnitude X-ray fluctuations on monthly-to-sub-year timescales, exceeding contemporaneous optical variations. Meanwhile, the radio flux density remains stable at $\sim2$ mJy across all ASKAP observations since mid-2020. Together with optical/UV and MIR variability and the broad He II transition, these results favor intrinsic accretion-state changes as the primary driver, while allowing a secondary contribution from variable obscuration. The source displays a loop-like MIR color--magnitude evolution, likely driven by the delayed response of an extended torus. This recurrent CLAGN offers a laboratory for probing the dynamic response of the broad-line region and circumnuclear dust to accretion-state transitions.
reference: Jiahua Wu, Liming Dou, Yanli Ai et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.04236.

title: Photon arrival time lags in 3D radiative transfer with SKIRT
abstract: Reprocessed X-ray emission from cold material surrounding compact objects carries critical information about the geometry and physical state of the system. In particular, the Fe K$α$ fluorescence line provides a powerful diagnostic through its spectral and timing properties relative to the direct emission. Interpreting these observables requires self-consistent modelling of radiative transfer (RT) in three-dimensional (3D) space. We aim to implement photon arrival time lags in SKIRT, a Monte Carlo RT code, thereby enabling self-consistent modelling of both the spectral and timing properties of reprocessed emission in 3D space. We modified the code to accumulate photon path lengths over their lifetimes and convert them into arrival time lags relative to the direct emission. The implementation is validated using simple geometries and then applied to a realistic model of an active galactic nucleus (AGN), for which we compute the time-lag and energy distribution and the cross-correlation functions (CCFs) between the fluorescence line and broad bands. The simulations reproduce the expected time-lag distributions and their energy dependence for both free-electron scattering and the photoelectric absorption $+$ fluorescence. In the AGN application, the model naturally yields distinct lag components from the inner and outer structures, as well as energy-dependent time lags associated with the fluorescence line. The derived CCFs successfully recover both the peak time lag and its finite width, which arise from the extended geometry and intrinsic variability. In X-rays, this capability provides a robust framework for interpreting high-resolution spectroscopic data in conjunction with timing information from current and future missions such as XRISM and NewAthena. A wide range of applications is foreseen, including reverberation mapping studies of accreting systems.
reference: Yuto Mochizuki, Bert Vander Meulen, Masahiro Tsujimoto et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.04187.

title: UV spectra of little red dots: Broad-line N/C, gas recycling and black hole masses
abstract: Radiative-transfer models of supermassive black holes accreting inside dense gas cocoons reproduce the X-ray-to-near-infrared spectral energy distribution of "little red dots" (LRDs) using the code Sirocco. In the ultraviolet, these models also predict weak broad emission lines and a series of metal absorption lines, which deep spectroscopy from the JWST SPURS survey now detects in several LRDs. Here we use the models to interpret these features. We find that N and C ions of equal charge (3+ or 2+) occupy largely the same gas in the simulations, such that the combination of the broad N IV]/C IV and N III]/C III] flux ratios simultaneously constrains both the electron density and the N/C abundance ratio of the gas in the LRD proper. The nitrogen and carbon emission of SPURS-GN-2, an LRD at $z=7.19$, requires an order of magnitude nitrogen excess compared to the solar value, N/C $= 12^{+3}_{-2}$ (N/C)$_\odot$, in the broad-line gas with electron density $\log n_e = 9.7^{+0.3}_{-0.5}$ cm$^{-3}$. Thus, around half the broad-line CNO nuclei have passed through hydrogen burning. Because the ionised gas is replaced on a century timescale, sustaining this enrichment favours gas recycling. UV absorption lines test this independently. In two of the four LRDs, line blueshift velocities clearly increase with the photon energy required to ionise the absorber gas. In the models the absorption lines are spatially stratified, indicating that the gas is launched near the escape speed and slowed by gravity. In GN-2, where the measurement can be made, the inferred deceleration requires radiation pressure close to the Eddington limit of a $10^{6-7}$ M$_\odot$ black hole. The lines are also typically strongly saturated, making inferences of direct abundance ratios misleading.
reference: Albert Sneppen, Darach Watson, Lucy R. Ivey et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.05349.

title: Revisiting the Stellar-Dynamical Mass of the Central Black Hole in NGC 3227
abstract: We present a new stellar-dynamical mass for the supermassive black hole in the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 3227. We determined the line-of-sight velocity distributions of stars in the nuclear region of NGC 3227 using archival spatially-resolved $K$-band spectra obtained with NIFS at Gemini Observatory. The surface brightness profile of the galaxy is described by four components, measured from a WFC3 F547M image from the Hubble Space Telescope. We constructed dynamical models using the Schwarzschild orbit-superposition method implemented in the open-source code $\texttt{FORSTAND}$. We find a best-fit black hole mass of $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$=$(1.2\pm0.5) \times 10^7$ $M_{\odot}$. This mass is consistent with a previous mass from R. I. Davies et al. based on stellar dynamics using orbit-based modeling, but our results make use of higher signal-to-noise data from which the higher-order moments of the stellar LOSVDs are constrained, thus providing a more precise $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$. Our result is also consistent with the $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$ constraint from velocity-resolved reverberation mapping reported by M. C. Bentz et al.. And while our best-fit mass is slightly smaller than the mass constraint from gas-dynamical modeling reported by E. K. S. Hicks & M. A. Malkan (after scaling to the same adopted distance), they are within 2$σ$ of each other. Direct comparisons of black hole masses from different techniques are rare but crucial to ensure all black hole masses are on the same scale, and to identify and minimize the uncertainties and possible sources of bias associated with each technique.
reference: Nabanita Das, Misty C. Bentz, Eugene Vasiliev et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.05547.

title: How Fast do Black Holes Spin?
abstract: We present a systematic study of the spin evolution of accreting black holes. Using the BHAC code for general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we conduct a total of 500 high resolution simulations of magnetized accretion disks around Kerr BHs with spin parameters ranging from $χ=0$ to $χ= 0.99$. The baseline configuration follows the default Fishbone--Moncrief torus setup in BHAC. We further explore the effects of: I) introducing multiple poloidal magnetic loops, II) the initial position of the torus, III) magnetic field strength and IV) radial loop modulation. From each simulation we extract the mass flux and angular momentum flux through the horizon to compute the time-averaged spin evolution rate after the system becomes quasi-stationary. The equilibrium spin ranges from $χ_{\rm eq}\simeq0.88$ in the fiducial model to $χ_{\rm eq}\simeq0.98$ for weak-flux model. Applied to Sgr A$^*$, even an optimistic estimate for rapid spin evolution gives a timescale longer than $10^{13}$ yr, indicating an earlier growth or merger history. These trends are consistent with the picture that larger net magnetic flux threading the horizon enhances jet-torques and reduces the equilibrium spins, whereas weak net flux yields near-maximal spins. Our results provide a pathway to interpret the high spins reported for X-ray binaries and active galactic nuclei and they sharpen the astrophysical viability of near-horizon high-energy processes that rely on near-extremal black holes.
reference: Chen Yuan, Vitor Cardoso (2026), arXiv:2611.04361.

title: Beyond just a torus? Re-contextualising the AGN type paradigm using data-driven host galaxy quenching histories
abstract: The orientation of a dusty torus within a unified model explains the presence (Type-1) or absence (Type-2) of broad emission lines in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) spectra. This orientation-based unified model, however, fails to explain differences in host galaxy properties, such as star formation rates, of Type-1 and Type-2 AGNs. Star-formation histories (SFHs) can shed light on the connection between AGN type and host galaxy properties, but are challenging to extract from Type-1 AGN that outshine their host galaxies. We use mean-field independent component analysis (MFICA) spectrum decomposition to extract the stellar populations of $\sim$3000 optically selected Type-1 and Type-2 AGN host galaxies from the seventh data release (DR7) of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), matched in redshift ($0.16 \leq z \leq 0.4$) and AGN luminosity ($6.5<\log_{10} [L_{[OIII]}/L_\odot] <9.5$). Using MFICA, we find that only $\sim$10 per cent of AGN host galaxies have recently ($\lesssim1$\,Gyr) and rapidly quenched star formation following a starburst, with Type-2 AGN host galaxies having done so at most 100\,Myrs more recently than Type-1 AGN host galaxies. For most ($\sim$90 per cent) AGN hosts with normal recent star formation histories, Type-2 AGNs are associated with slightly younger stellar populations than Type-1 AGNs. The younger stellar populations of Type-2 AGN hosts can be explained by a link between dusty torus covering factors and stellar populations, by host-galaxy obscuration of AGN, or by an evolution in AGN type without major bursts or rapid quenching of star formation.
reference: Sahyadri D. Krishna, Vivienne Wild, Paul C. Hewett et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.05353.

title: A pocket of oxygen in a near-pristine galaxy at z=4.2: chemical inhomogeneity at 10-parsec scales in LAP2
abstract: We aim to constrain the oxygen abundance, the ionizing properties, and the spatial structure of LAP2, a strongly lensed (with a magnification $μ$~50) oxygen-deficient galaxy at z=4.2 behind the galaxy cluster Abell 2744. We present new JWST/NIRSpec IFU PRISM observations (~13.6 hr) of LAP2, which we combine with archival JWST/NIRCam imaging. LAP2 is intrinsically extremely faint (M_UV=-12.7) and has a low stellar mass (M~$10^5~M_\odot$), comparable to that of massive star clusters. It consists of a compact core ($R_{eff}$~7 pc) embedded in a more diffuse emission (with $R_{eff}$~20 pc). Strong H$α$ emission (EW$_{\rm rest}\simeq880$ Å, $\logξ_{\rm ion}\simeq25.3$), a blue UV slope ($β_{\rm UV}\simeq-2.5$, down to $\simeq-3.1$ in the core), and a Balmer decrement consistent with no dust attenuation indicate a young ($\lesssim10$ Myr), dust-free burst. [OIII]$λ$5007 is not detected in the integrated spectrum, implying [OIII]/H$β\leq0.61$ ($3σ$) and, using an extrapolated strong-line calibration, $12+\log({\rm O/H})\leq6.4$ ($\lesssim0.5\%\,Z_\odot$). This places LAP2 among the most metal-poor galaxies known. Faint [OIII] emission is, however, detected in the core (with $\rm4σ$ significance), where we derive $12+\log({\rm O/H})\simeq6.6$ ($\sim1\%\,Z_\odot$). This difference can be explained either by local self-enrichment, requiring only $\rm \sim0.2\,M_\odot$ of newly synthesized oxygen, or by a higher ionization parameter in the core. The upper limit on HeII$λ$1640 (EW$_{\rm rest}<39$ Å, $3σ$) does not exclude a contribution from metal-free stars. LAP2 extends the census of spectroscopically confirmed EMPGs to star-cluster masses and to $M_{\rm UV}\approx-13$. Its location in a low-density region supports a scenario in which underdense environments preserve nearly pristine gas well after reionization.
reference: M. Messa, E. Vanzella, S. Rojas-Ruiz et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.05487.

title: Euclid. Predicting scaling relations for emission-line galaxies using simulated data
abstract: The Euclid spectroscopic surveys will substantially increase the number of observed emission-line galaxies. We assess the ability of the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and Euclid Deep Survey (EDS), at the final DR3 depth, to recover the star-forming main sequence (MS), dust-mass relation (DMR), and mass-metallicity relation (MZR) from emission-line measurements. We use MAMBO (mocks with abundance matching in Bologna) spectroscopic simulations processed with the official Euclid pipelines. The MS is traced over $0\leq z\leq 4$ using Pa$β$, H$α$, and [OII] as SFR tracers. The shallow EWS flux limit biases the MS towards higher normalisation and a flatter slope by selecting the brightest, most strongly star-forming galaxies. The deeper EDS enables almost complete sampling with Pa$β$ and H$α$ at log$_{10}(M_*/M_\odot)\geq10.3$ over $0\leq z\leq 1.88$, with mild biases at both redshift limits. The [OII]-based MS is increasingly biased towards higher SFRs at the highest redshifts. The DMR is traced through the Balmer decrement over $1.45\leq z\leq 1.88$ and $0.9\leq z\leq 1.88$ in the EWS and EDS, respectively. The derived colour excess agree well with the input values, although detecting the faint H$β$ line restricts the sample to less obscured galaxies at fixed $M_*$, particularly in the EWS; the DMR is better sampled in the EDS. Finally, a golden sample detected in multiple optical rest-frame emission lines at $1.49\leq z\leq 1.88$ recovers gas-phase metallicities with typical accuracy of 0.1 dex at log$_{10}(M_*/M_\odot)\geq10$, while lower-mass galaxies show biases up to 0.15 dex. Relative to H-band limited sample, this sample preferentially traces the upper MS and lower MZR. Despite the simplified simulations lacking effects such as mutual spectral contamination and detector persistence, these forecasts provide a benchmark for future Euclid spectroscopic analyses.
reference: Euclid Collaboration, C. Mancini, L. Gabarra et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.05482.

title: ReveaLLAGN 2: Exploring the Nuclear Gas and Stellar Kinematics of Nearby LLAGNs with JWST/NIRSpec IFU
abstract: Low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGN) represent the most common mode of black hole accretion in the local Universe, yet their nuclear structure, stellar and gas kinematics remain poorly constrained at parsec scales. We investigate the nuclear regions of eight nearby representative LLAGN, the ReveaLLAGN sample: M87, M104, M94, M81, NGC1052, NGC4258, NGC5128 and NGC4395. Using JWST/NIRSpec data, we probe the stellar, molecular hydrogen, hydrogen recombination, and high ionisation coronal lines kinematics and their spatial distribution, exploring how detectability and spatial distributions of these lines vary across different Eddington ratios. The stellar LOSV maps reveal a slowly rotating disk in the nuclei of all our targets, characterised by an anti-correlation with the h3 Gauss-Hermite moment. Across the sample, the stellar velocity dispersion rises toward the central black hole. Only in M104 and M94 does the velocity dispersion display a more intricate pattern that departs from a simple disk configuration, indicating the presence of multiple kinematic components in these galaxies. Across the sample, the gas distribution and kinematics exhibit rotation that is frequently decoupled from the stellar rotation, suggesting that the stellar gravitational potential is decoupled from the current accretion state. The gas kinematics are often visually aligned with the radio jet, presenting broader velocity dispersions along the jet direction. Line-ratio maps indicate that the dominant excitation mechanism is photoionisation by the central AGN, with mechanical heating from shocks becoming important only at higher Eddington ratios. Across the sample, we detect coronal lines in all LLAGN when using nuclear-aperture spectra, and we can obtain spatially resolved kinematics only in NGC5128 and NGC4395, the highest Eddington ratio sources.
reference: Antoine Dumont, Nadine Neumayer, Anil C. Seth et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.05496.

title: Black Hole Mass Estimation of a Background Quasar in the Vicinity of the cD Galaxy Holm 15A
abstract: This study analyzes spectra from the central region of the galaxy cluster Abell 85 observed with GTC/OSIRIS, focusing on the cD galaxy Holm 15A and the point-like X-ray source SDSS J004150.75-091824.3, projected $13.74\arcsec$ from Holm 15A. For the latter, we found it is a background quasar with a redshift of $1.56386 \pm 0.00397$, ruling out the possibility of it being a rogue BH gravitationally bound to Holm 15A. In addition, using single-epoch spectroscopy, we report that the quasar J004150 hosts a Supermassive Black Hole (SMBH) with a mass of $\log(M_{\text{BH}}/\mathrm{M_{\odot}}) = 8.72 \pm 0.26$.
reference: Emmanuel Ríos-López, Omar López-Cruz, Ana Luisa González-Morán et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.05316.

title: SN 2019qem: decades of extreme mass loss before the explosion of a luminous, long-lived Type IIn supernova
abstract: We present the luminous, long-lived Type IIn SN 2019qem and use it to reconstruct how much mass its progenitor lost and when. We combine host-subtracted optical and mid-infrared photometry and 26 optical spectra from -22 to +699 d. We model the bolometric light curve with thin-shell CSM-interaction models in REDBACK, with the shock velocity constrained by the H$α$ line widths, and compare them with an analytic interaction model. SN 2019qem rose in $\approx30$d to $M_I = -20.5$mag and a bolometric peak of $7.0\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and radiated $6.9\times10^{50}$ erg in the optical within 575 d, closely resembling luminous, strongly interacting SNe IIn such as SN 2010jl and SN 2015da. A Heii/Niii flash feature at -22 d and unresolved narrow Balmer lines reveal dense, slow CSM. From +78 to +445 d the H$α$ wings are shaped by electron scattering, and the line stays blueshifted by 400-700 km s$^{-1}$, which points to an optically thick, asymmetric interaction region rather than to newly formed dust. In the preferred model, $\approx7 M_\odot$ of ejecta run into $\approx9 M_\odot$ of gas ejected $\approx2$ yr before explosion and then into a wind of $\approx0.6 M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ (for $v_w = 100$ km s$^{-1}$), sweeping up $\approx32 M_\odot$ by +544 d. The mid-infrared excess brightens for two years while the optical fades, tracing dust heated by the ongoing interaction. The host is a low-mass, star-forming galaxy, $\log(M_*/M_\odot) = 9.19$, with a sub-solar metallicity at the explosion site. In its final decades the progenitor of SN 2019qem lost mass far faster than any steady stellar wind, ending with an eruption of $\approx9 M_\odot$ two years before core collapse, consistent with luminous-blue-variable-like eruptive mass loss. Taken at face value, the mass budget implies an initial progenitor mass of $\gtrsim40 M_\odot$.
reference: Joysankar Majumdar, Mariusz Gromadzki, Takashi J. Moriya et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.05328.

title: HI Emission Recovery in the Low-Redshift Radio Population: Host-Galaxy and Radio-Luminosity Dependence in FASHI and LoTSS
abstract: Overlapping blind 21 cm and wide-area low-frequency continuum surveys make it possible to measure which radio sources an untargeted HI survey recovers. Cross-matching FASHI DR1 with the LoTSS DR2 value-added catalog yields 4392 one-to-one associations. Within an empirically defined comparison region of $2912$\,deg$^2$, we construct a low-redshift, spectroscopic, radio-selected parent of 25,573 LoTSS sources whose expected HI line falls in the FASHI band, and measure how often each is recovered. Sources classified as radio-loud AGN in the published LoTSS DR2 radio-AGN classification are recovered less often than star-forming ones: 143 of 1542 ($9.27\%$, $7.87$--$10.83$) against $14.88\%$ ($14.43$--$15.33$) of 24,031, an odds ratio of $0.585$ ($0.491$--$0.697$). The two classes, however, differ strongly in host properties, by $1.34$ dex in median specific star formation rate, and within their overlapping stellar-mass and star-formation ranges we detect no statistically significant residual class difference (adjusted odds ratio $1.60$, $0.87$--$2.94$). In contrast, 144 MHz luminosity remains positively associated with HI recovery after adjustment for the measured host properties, redshift and an approximate sensitivity proxy: within the same overlapping range, each dex raises the odds of recovery by a factor of $2.03$ ($1.54$--$2.68$), an association carried primarily by the star-forming population, not by the radio-AGN subsample. We interpret this as an empirical relationship with detectable HI emission, not as evidence that radio activity increases or decreases HI mass. The association catalog and the controlled recovery measurements characterize the radio population sampled by a blind HI survey.
reference: Soumen Kumar Bera, Taotao Fang, Chuan He et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.04351.

title: Decomposition of disk and jet optical emission: Case of PKS~1510-089 and PKS~0736+017
abstract: Measuring BLR size and black hole mass of jetted quasars with strong radio emission is challenging due to the contribution from non-thermal synchrotron radiation from the jet in the optical continuum. Here, we investigate the optical continuum emission in two flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), PKS~0736+017 and PKS~1510-089, by separating the thermal emission from the accretion disk and the non-thermal synchrotron emission from the jet using their distinct polarization signatures. Our analysis combines multi-epoch optical spectro-photometric and polarimetric observations from the archival optical continuum, H$β$ emission line light curves from earlier reverberation mapping campaigns, and 37 GHz radio data. For PKS~0736+017, we find that the disk contributes approximately 70 % ($f_d = 0.70^{+0.01}_{-0.01}$) of the total optical emission. After removing the jet component, we obtain a revised H$β$ lag of $84.8^{+23.2}_{-18.4}$ days. In contrast, the disk contribution in PKS~1510-089 is lower with 37.5 % ($f_d = 0.37^{+0.01}_{-0.01}$), with a corresponding H$β$ lag of $54.4^{+4.4}_{-5.4}$ days. Our findings highlight the need for careful decomposition of optical light curves in jet-dominated AGN.
reference: Shivangi Pandey, Suvendu Rakshit, Adarsh Kumar et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.03006.

title: X-rays from Low-mass Active Galaxies in the Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) Survey
abstract: We present new Chandra observations of seven broad-line AGNs in low-mass galaxies ($M_\star < 5 \times 10^9\,M_\odot$) selected from the GAMA sample of Salehirad et al. (2022). X-ray emission is detected in six galaxies, with luminosities spanning $\log(L_{\rm 0.5-8\,keV}/{\rm erg\,s^{-1}})\approx40.5$--43.8. Their X-ray luminosities generally exceed predictions for X-ray binary populations, and their proximity to the optical galaxy nuclei favors accreting massive black holes as the dominant emission source. Spectral fits for four sources yield photon indices $Γ\approx1.7$--2.2, with little evidence for intrinsic absorption in most cases. Virial black hole masses and hard X-ray bolometric corrections imply nominal Eddington ratios $λ_{\rm Edd}\approx0.004$--1.1, although uncertainties are substantial. Optical tracers generally imply higher bolometric luminosities and Eddington ratios, particularly for the X-ray-undetected galaxy. The X-ray-bright sources are broadly consistent with optical AGN scaling relations involving H$α$ and [O III], whereas most lie below the established X-ray--mid-infrared relation, potentially reflecting host-galaxy contamination. Four sources are consistent with the expected UV-to-X-ray spectral slope relation, while three show evidence for relative X-ray weakness. These results reveal diverse X-ray properties among broad-line AGNs in low-mass galaxies and highlight the importance of multiwavelength diagnostics for understanding black hole accretion and interpreting broad-line AGN candidates at high redshift.
reference: Stellan Bechtold, Amy Reines, Richard Plotkin et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.03820.

title: Ly$α$ in Compact Broad-Line Emitters, Including Little Red Dots, Is More Closely Linked to the Host Galaxy than to the Broad-Line Nucleus
abstract: JWST has found many faint broad-line AGN at $z>4$, but it is unclear whether the Ly$α$ we see from them comes from the accreting black hole or from its host galaxy. The answer matters for how these sources are interpreted and for how many ionizing photons they release. We use deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the DIVER program to measure Ly$α$ in 12 compact broad-line emitters (CBEs) at $z=4.2$--5.5 in GOODS-N. CBEs include little red dots (LRDs), little blue dots, and other broad-line AGN. Six are detected in Ly$α$. Every source shows a broad-line region, yet Ly$α$ does not follow it: the sources with the strongest H$α$ relative to the UV include weak detections and nondetections, and every detected Ly$α$ line (FWHM $\approx300$--1000~km~s$^{-1}$) is narrower than broad H$α$ (1100--3300~km~s$^{-1}$). Instead, Ly$α$ appears to track the host galaxy. We model the AGN-subtracted host with a dust-attenuated SED fit. Including the upper limits, the observed Ly$α$ follows the Ly$α$ production in this host model more closely than it follows H$α$/UV, in both equivalent width and luminosity. Every detection exceeds its host-model value by a factor of 1.5--18, leaving room for a nuclear contribution. The black hole is visible in these sources, but the Ly$α$ we observe is more closely tied to its host. The median effective Ly$α$ escape fraction of the detections is only 0.09, which suggests that ionizing escape from CBEs is typically modest and varies widely.
reference: Yongda Zhu, Zheng Ma, Xiaojing Lin et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.03801.

title: An Empirical Temperature Relation for Chemical Abundances in AGN
abstract: We present for the very first time the empirical temperature structure of the narrow line region (NLR) clouds of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) based on a sample of [N II] and [O III] auroral line measurements. The scaling of Te([N II]) with Te([O III]), expressed as the t2-t3 relation, is key to deriving accurate chemical abundances, in AGNs and other line-emitting nebulae, particularly when only one auroral line is observed. Here, we provide the first robust empirical description of t2-t3 for AGNs: t2(10^4 K)=1.285*t3(10^4 K)+0.799. We find substantial changes in 12+log(O/H) when compared to other t2-t3 calibrations when using the direct, or Te, method with only the [O III] 4363 auroral line. We find that adopting our t2-t3 most accurately recovers the fully direct method 12+log(O/H). To interpret the physical mechanisms behind the AGN t2-t3, we compare the observed distribution of [N II] 6584/5755 and [O III] 5007/4363 flux ratios to a variety of ionization model predictions. We find evidence for power law density gradients, pressure stratification, and (sometimes significant) contributions from astrophysical shocks driving much of the dispersion on these flux ratios while metal cooling dominates the primary shape of the distribution. With more accurate t2-t3 and 12+log(O/H), the properties of the interstellar medium photoionized by AGN can be better characterized and understood across a wide range of cosmic time and may bring better context for novel observations at z>6 with JWST, with implications for understanding chemical enrichment in the earliest stages of galaxy evolution.
reference: Sophia R. Flury, Oli L. Dors, Rogemar A. Riffel et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.02915.

title: A magnetically heated slim disc-corona model for tidal disruption events
abstract: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) can reach super-Eddington luminosities near their peak. While their optical/UV emission may arise from multiple processes, X-rays are more likely to be produced by the innermost accretion flow close to the black hole, analogous to super-Eddington flows in stellar-mass X-ray binaries (XRBs) and active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Super-Eddington AGNs typically show disc-dominated spectra, with weak and steep coronae, while super-Eddington XRBs show a wider variety of spectral shapes. Here we explore disc-corona coupling in TDEs by developing a super-Eddington ($\dot{m}>1$: slim) disc model in which magnetic reconnection transfers some of the accretion power from the disc into a hot Comptonizing corona. We test the model on the well-monitored X-ray TDE AT2021ehb, and can broadly fit the brightest X-ray spectra with a black-hole mass $M_{\rm BH}\sim10^6$--$10^7\,M_\odot$ at $\dot m\sim 1$, but need variable magnetic coupling to the disc to match the large observed fast changes in coronal contribution. AGN at similarly high luminosity do not show such variable coronae, but the transient XRB outbursts do, suggesting that it may be a common feature of rapidly changing, non-steady accretion flows. As the TDE declines to $\dot{m}\sim 0.01$, the source hardens, but never goes below $Γ\sim 2$, unlike both AGN and XRB at these luminosities. Thus the X-ray spectral evolution in this TDE does not resemble either XRB or AGN in detail, likely pointing to the very different, highly variable nature of the accretion flow in a tidal disruption event.
reference: Wei Chen, Chris Done, Erlin Qiao et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.02445.

title: H 0557$-$385: A Candidate Missing Link Between Radio-Quiet Seyferts and Young Radio Galaxies
abstract: The Seyfert 1 galaxy H 0557$-$385 (z = 0.034) has long been classified as radio-quiet on the basis of its radio-to-optical flux ratio, yet its radio properties are physically inconsistent with this designation. We present a broadband ($0.076 - 258.8$ GHz) radio spectral analysis combining new Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) observations with archival Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) data. The spectrum requires a two-component model: a compact, self-absorbed component with a stratified gigahertz-peaked (GPS)/high-frequency-peaked (HFP) spectral shape (turnover at $9.4^{+0.6}_{-0.5}$ GHz), superposed on an extended, optically thin power-law lobe ($α_{\rm pl} = -0.78$) that dominates below ~1.6 GHz. The derived parameters $-$ a source size of ~15 pc, an equipartition magnetic field of 2.8 mG, a synchrotron age of $\lesssim1.8\times10^{3}$ yr, and a time-averaged jet power of ${\sim}5\times10^{41}$ $-$ $5\times10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$ $-$ are characteristic of compact steep-spectrum and GPS young radio galaxies, not of canonical radio-quiet AGN. The two-component structure admits two interpretations that the present data cannot distinguish: the extended emission may be the growing lobe of a genuinely young, expanding radio galaxy, or relic plasma from an earlier episode of a transient or recurrent jet. Under either, H 0557$-$385 is better understood as an intermediate object: optically a Seyfert, but with the radio-physical properties of a newly ignited or recently re-triggered radio galaxy. It is therefore a candidate missing link between radio-quiet AGN and large-scale radio galaxies. Distinguishing these scenarios will require high-resolution imaging and multi-epoch monitoring
reference: J. Chauhan, T. D. Russell, A. Lohfink et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.03818.

title: Evidence for strong shocks in the ISM of small radio sources
abstract: Radio jets deposit energy into the interstellar medium of their host galaxies, and while a jet is still confined within the host it is expected to drive shocks through the gas. Broad [OIII] 5007 profiles trace ionized gas that has been disturbed, the [OI]/H-alpha versus [OIII]/H-beta diagram helps distinguish gas photoionized by an AGN from gas excited by shocks, and the high ionization [NeV] 3426 line traces the hard UV continuum of the accretion disk, which shocks only reproduce at very high velocities. We have selected two samples of radio-loud AGN from a cross-match of the VLA Sky Survey with DESI Data Release 1, at 0.15 < z < 0.5 and with [OI] 6300 detected at > 5-sigma: one with projected radio sizes of 10-15 kpc, whose jets are still inside the host, and one with sizes greater than 25 kpc, whose jets have broken out. We fit the [OIII] and [OI] profiles, measure W80, and classify each source on the BPT diagram. The confined sources have broader [OIII] lines, sit systematically closer to the LINER region, and are detected less often in [NeV], and the [NeV] difference is not explained by redshift or dust. The broad components are not systematically blueshifted, so the confined sources are distinguished by line width rather than by outflow velocity. We then discuss how these results indicate that the jets of the confined sources are driving strong shocks through the interstellar medium of their hosts.
reference: Valeria Lopez, Mark Lacy (2026), arXiv:2611.03848.

title: Jets and winds from the most powerful compact object in NGC 5408
abstract: Super-critical accretion onto stellar-mass compact objects is sometimes revealed by ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs). In other cases, X-rays are heavily obscured along our line of sight, but a super-Eddington accretion power can be indirectly revealed by multiband studies. We have identified a candidate super-critical source in NGC 5408 (labelled X-2). We argue that: it is powered by accretion; it is among the most powerful in the local universe, despite its apparent X-ray faintness; it has exceptional optical properties (both in the continuum and in the lines). We carried out a multiband imaging and spectral study with the ATCA, the VLA, HST, the VLT and Chandra. We found an unresolved source with: variable radio emission (5-GHz luminosity of a few x 10^{35} erg/s); red optical continuum with absolute mag M_{V,0} = -9.1, M_{I,0} = -10.6; exceptionally broad low-ionization emission lines (FWHM ~ 1700 km/s) with P-Cygni profiles; narrow, photoionized emission lines including strong He II 4686; point-like hard X-rays; marginally resolved soft X-rays. We also found an ~20-pc He^{++} nebula near X-2, associated with candidate Wolf-Rayet stars. The optical continuum declined by 2 mag between 2010 and 2024, as did the intensity of broad and narrow lines. We argue that the system is powered by the radiative and mechanical output of a super-Eddington stellar mass BH, with an accretion power >~10^{40} erg/s. We propose that X-2 is a Compton-thick ULX seen at high inclination, with a flaring jet and X-ray emission emerging from the polar funnel. We argue that the optical continuum and the broad emission lines are signatures of an optically thick outflow, launched either from the accretion disk, or from an LBV-like donor star, or, more speculatively, caused by the elusive phase of common envelope ejection. We suggest that we are looking at a short-lived phase of hyper-Eddington accretion.
reference: Roberto Soria, Manfred W. Pakull, Christian Motch et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.03796.

title: How bursty star formation shapes spectral diversity at high redshifts: breaking degeneracies in early galaxy formation
abstract: JWST has revealed an unexpected abundance of z>10 galaxies and striking spectral diversity. Here, we model bursty star formation histories (SFHs) to explore how they shape this diversity and whether spectroscopy can discriminate between explanations for the UV luminosity function (UVLF) excess. We find strong burstiness ($σ_{UV}(M_h=10^{10}M_\odot)$~0.9 mag), increasing toward low halo masses, is required to reproduce the z~6 UVLF and observed fractions of galaxies in recent star formation upturns and downturns, traced by SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}$. This burstiness naturally reproduces UVLFs and SFR upturn and downturn fractions over z~6-11. With increasing redshift, we predict galaxies in recent upturns (SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}>5$) increasingly dominate the UVLF bright end, reflecting rising accretion rates and burstier low-mass halos. This results in higher median emission-line equivalent widths (EWs), bluer UV slopes and weaker Balmer breaks at fixed $M_{UV}$, while distributions of these properties broaden. We find the downturn fraction (SFR$_3$/SFR$_{50}<0.2$) is particularly sensitive to stochasticity: increasing towards faint $M_{UV}$ if burstiness increases in lower mass halos, and evolving with redshift only if stochasticity does. However, the model underpredicts the z~14 UVLF, so we explore two models which match the UVLF: increased burstiness and increased star formation efficiency. From z=10 to 14, at fixed $M_{UV}$, increased burstiness predicts the downturn fraction increases by ~2x and the weak-emitter fraction (H$β$ EW<50Å) by ~1.5x. By contrast, the increased efficiency model predicts a constant downturn fraction and declining weak-emitter fraction. Overall, our results indicate burstiness is important for explaining spectral diversity and evolution at z~6-14, and that spectroscopic samples spanning a broad $M_{UV}$ range can establish its role in the z~14 UVLF excess.
reference: Viola Gelli, Charlotte A. Mason, Daniel P. Stark et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.03790.

title: Stellar wind variability in OB stars and its effect on mass-loss determinations
abstract: Virtually all stellar winds of OB stars exhibit variability in one spectral diagnostic or another. This review focuses primarily on UV spectroscopic signatures of this variability and on studies that have exploited it to reveal the presence of large-scale velocity and density structures in the winds. The review includes demonstrations that the physical structures responsible for the variations appear to be large, spatially coherent and rooted in the stellar photospheres. Furthermore, evidence is summarised that these structures can be optically thick to resonance line radiation and are dense enough to modulate the X-ray fluxes that originate in the wind. Also discussed, is how the structures can affect wind line formation and, as a result, the precision by which mass-loss rates can be determined. The potential of millimetre and radio continuum observations to constrain the radial stratification of wind clumping is highlighted, as a future path to reliable empirical determinations of massive star mass-loss rates.
reference: Raman K. Prinja (2026), arXiv:2611.03363.

title: An all-sky catalogue of Be transition stars from WISE and Gaia
abstract: We present an all-sky catalogue of classical Be stars undergoing transitions between quiescent B-type and active Be-star phases, based on Gaia DR3 astrometry and multi-epoch mid-infrared photometry from WISE and NEOWISE-R. From a Gaia-selected parent sample of 4.2 million candidate OBA stars, we identify Be transition stars through correlated variability in $W_1$ magnitude and $W_1-W_2$ colour, which traces circumstellar disk formation and dissipation. The final catalogue contains 3,300 Be transition stars, including 2,743 newly identified objects, and provides a large, homogeneous sample for studying Be outburst activity across the sky. The median durations of the measured outburst and decay phases are 459 and 478 days, respectively, consistent with previous WISE-based measurements and compatible with the long disk-evolution timescales expected in the viscous decretion disk framework. As an initial application, we use TESS photometry for 3,017 targets to identify 63 eclipsing binary systems hosting Be transition stars, including 33 Algol-type, 17 Beta Lyrae-type, and 13 W Ursae Majoris-type systems. Among the multi-epoch LAMOST spectra, two sources show candidate radial-velocity shifts exceeding 20 km s $^{-1}$; their line-profile behaviour suggests that RV variability in active Be transition stars may be influenced by outburst-related line-profile changes rather than being an unambiguous indicator of binary motion. This catalogue provides a basis for future statistical studies of Be outbursts, disk evolution, and their connection with binarity and spectroscopic variability.
reference: Qi Jia, Mingjie Jian, Gang Li et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.02450.

title: A Cepheid-based Distance to the Type 1 Seyfert NGC 3783
abstract: We present a Cepheid-based distance to the Type 1 Seyfert NGC 3783 using the Hubble Space Telescope. Images were obtained over 15 visits using nonredundant time spacing, with ten observations in the F350LP filter and eight observations each in the F555W and F814W filters. We found 1541 unique point sources across all observations, and we fit Cepheid templates to analyze these light curves. From these data, we determined a full sample of seven Cepheid candidates. Of these seven candidates, four are the most convincing and comprise our "strong" sample of Cepheid candidates. We fit the period$-$luminosity relationship to the total sample and to our "strong" sample using the LMC calibration by Riess et al. (2019). Adopting an independent distance constraint to the LMC given by Pietrzynski et al. (2019), and correcting for the potential effects of metallicity, we determine a distance modulus of $μ= 33.118 \pm 0.154$ mag using our strong sample. This value is formally consistent with the value derived using our full sample and corresponds to a distance of $D = 42.03 \pm 2.98$ Mpc. NGC 3783 is therefore among the farthest galaxies with a Cepheid-based distance measurement.
reference: Madison Markham, Misty C. Bentz, Laura Ferrarese et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.03226.

title: GALACTIC CENTERS AS TRACERS OF GALAXY EVOLUTION: Zooming from galaxy large-scale properties into their central massive black holes
abstract: During the workshop ''Galactic Centers as tracers of galaxy evolution'' (Lorentz Center, Leiden), we reviewed one of the most debated questions in the field of galaxy evolution: the connection between galactic central regions and the evolution of galaxies at a global scale. We gathered different research communities to reveal the connection channels between central massive black holes (MBHs), nuclear structures, and evolutionary processes at a global scale, such as gas inflows and outflows and galaxy-galaxy interactions. Special focus was dedicated to MBH seeding, formation and growth, active galactic nuclei feedback, and the formation of nuclear stellar structures, without missing a global perspective. Participants from these different fields introduced us to the state of the art in numerical simulations, as well as cutting-edge observational techniques. In addition to achieving a deep understanding of these topics, we set up plans to exploit future facilities such as the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). In this paper, we briefly summarize the highlights of the workshop, identify the open questions that emerged during the workshop discussions, and discuss what observations and simulations will be needed to address them.
reference: F. Pinna, N. Hoyer, S. Thater et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.03090.

title: Witnessing pre-processing at intermediate redshift: observational evidence of infalling groups onto a merging galaxy cluster
abstract: The fraction of quenched galaxies increases with local density, and part of this trend is thought to arise in groups before cluster accretion (pre-processing). In merging clusters, this is difficult to separate from star formation triggered or suppressed by the cluster merger itself. We investigate whether five high-velocity galaxies in the merging cluster SPT-CL~J0307-6225 ($z=0.579$), distributed in two candidate infalling groups, show signs of group-scale environmental processing prior to accretion. We combine MUSE integral-field spectroscopy and HST imaging to derive [\ion{O}{ii}] kinematic maps, spectral classes, and star-formation rates (SFR), to understand the properties of the galaxies. We further use the Magneticum simulations and the phase-space information to determine if these galaxies are part of two groups, and if they will be accreted onto the merging cluster. Group~1 is a morphologically disturbed interacting pair bound to the cluster, with at least one galaxy classified as dusty starburst. Group~2 is a compact triplet at $\sim$4$σ_v$ from the cluster, in which two galaxies share a common [\ion{O}{ii}] envelope and the dominant member, an e(b) starburst, shows an elevated ionised-gas velocity dispersion. The SFR of both starburst galaxies lie within the scatter of the field star-forming main sequence, as expected for modest, interaction-triggered bursts. Close pairs at the phase-space position of group~2 occur for $\sim$1\% of comparable-mass cluster galaxies in Magneticum, so it is not unlikely for the group to be bound. Both groups show spatially resolved signatures of galaxy--galaxy interactions alongside ongoing star formation, supporting a pre-processing scenario in the environment of a merging cluster. Such group-scale interactions may contribute to the enhanced star formation reported in merging clusters.
reference: D. Hernández-Lang, D. Pallero, A. Ivleva et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.01344.

title: EMU/GAMA: Understanding the link between dust geometry and star formation rate in galaxies
abstract: We investigate the link between dust obscuration and star formation rate (SFR) estimators using Halpha luminosities, L_Halpha and radio luminosities, L_radio. While the Balmer Decrement (BD) is the standard tool for attenuating Halpha, it can fail to account for optically thick dust regions from which Halpha cannot escape. The ratio of SFRs estimated from radio luminosity and L_Halpha corrected for dust attenuation using the BD can be used as a probe of the degree of optically thick dust affecting Halpha. We explore this combining Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) Early Science data at 887.5MHz in the Galaxy and Mass Assembly (GAMA) G23 field with the GAMA data. We draw on dust estimates using both the BD and the dust mass, M_d, demonstrating systematic underlying dependencies with L_radio/L_Halpha. By combining the BD and M_d, we quantify how they relate to L_radio/L_Halpha and other galaxy properties. We use this approach to establish an Halpha SFR (SFR_Halpha) estimator that accounts for optically thick dust, demonstrating its consistency with conventional SFR indicators. Rather than proposing a replacement for standard correction methods, we aim to demonstrate the effectiveness of a dust geometry model that integrates both BD and M_d parameters. This H_dust parameter provides a more physically complete representation of optically thick environments that traditional methods may overlook, and can produce SFR estimates consistent with traditional techniques.
reference: U. T. Ahmed, A. M. Hopkins, B. Farley et al. (2026), arXiv:2611.00741.

title: The Broad-Line Region Size-Luminosity Relation in AGN Constrained by the Viewing Angle with the FRADO Model
abstract: We investigate the H$β$ broad-line region (BLR) size-luminosity ($R_{\rm BLR}$-$L_{5100}$) relation of active galactic nuclei (AGN) using a Bayesian viewing angle inference framework based on the Failed Radiatively Accelerated Dusty Outflow (FRADO) model. First, we update the FRADO model by introducing a phase factor to account for the anisotropic visibility of the illuminated cloud surface. Second, we construct a Bayesian framework to constrain the viewing angle by matching the FRADO-based $R_{\rm BLR}$ to the measured H$β$ lags of 151 AGN from Wang & Woo (2024). We successfully reproduce the slope and intrinsic scatter of the observed $R_{\rm BLR}$-$L_{5100}$ relation, finding that the inferred viewing angles are broadly consistent with the estimates from dynamical modeling of velocity-resolved reverberation data, albeit with substantial scatter. As the observed H$β$ time lag and line velocity depend on the viewing angle, the black hole mass ($M_{\rm BH}$) calibrated from our work is typically larger than the reverberation-mapping estimates using an average virial factor.
